ann_120.original: Capital gains pull the prediction away from a low income, and the pull steepens once gains pass about $4,000. Self-probe (the typical person: a married husband, high-school graduate, with no gains or losses, gains swept): this part's contribution to the low-income score goes from 1.36 at no gains to 0.60 at $3,500, -0.12 at $5,000 and -4.00 at $10,000: it falls slowly up to $3,500 and much faster beyond $5,000; in the whole model the predicted chance of a low income falls from 72% to 55%, 37% and 1.2%. The bend is two stacked hinges. Node 1266 is off at $3,500 (pre-activation -0.037) and on at $4,000 (0.028); node 8342, fed by 1266, is still off at $4,500 (pre-activation -0.037) and on at $5,000 (0.021). Both feed the output with negative weights, adding to the direct edge from capital gains (weight -3.11 per sd), while node 194 (capital-gain weight 1.24 per sd) feeds the output with a positive weight and gives back part of the direct edge's slope. In the training data 1266 is on for 2356 people, whose mean predicted chance of a low income is 17% (observed 20%), and 8342 for 2016 (mean predicted 10%). Every training row with gains of $4,000 or more has 1266 on (0 rows with it off); 70 rows just below $4,000 also have it on. Node 194 is zero on 50 training rows, and the 50 people born in Iran are those rows (Iran-born rows with 194 above zero: 0): the Iran indicator (weight -0.49 per sd into 194) shuts the node, so these people lose its offset, a regime fitted to 50 rows. Capital losses enter through one direct edge (weight -0.28 per sd): for the typical person, losses of $1,000 and $2,000 lower the predicted chance of a low income from 72% to 56% and 39%. Switching this part off lowers the training AUC from 0.907 to 0.885.
ann_120.proposed: Capital gains lower the predicted chance of a low income slowly at first, then faster (for a typical person from about 72% to about 12% between 0 US dollars and 6849 US dollars), more steeply for people born in Iran, and capital losses lower it steadily (to about 41% at 1887 US dollars).

ann_121.original: This part carries marriage, household role and sex. The marriage edge has the largest weight here (-1.68 per sd for married, civilian spouse), followed by sex (-0.56 per sd, men coded 1) and the not-in-a-family edge (-0.45 per sd). Self-probe on the typical person (a married husband): this part contributes -1.81 to the low-income score and the predicted chance of a low income is 72%; the same man never married and living outside a family gets 0.76 (97%), and divorced and outside a family 0.46 (96%). A married woman recorded as wife gets -2.23 (63%), below the husband, and a never-married woman outside a family 1.94 (99%), so the model's sex gap reverses inside marriage and widens outside it. In the training data the 17,909 people married to a civilian spouse have a mean predicted chance of 52% against 94% for the other 21,164. The husband gate (node 17026) is on for the 15,748 husbands and for no one else (0 non-husbands with it on, 0 husbands with it off); it adds a small positive term (edge weight 0.205), and switching it off lowers the husbands' predicted chance of a low income by 1.4% (in probability) on average and leaves their AUC at 0.811. ann_127.original: The model predicts the chance of a low income ($50,000 a year or less) as a sigmoid of a score that is a plain sum of the exits of the seven child parts and a bias; no part feeds another, so the parts' effects add on the score, and on the probability scale the sigmoid makes them interact. On the training split the model has an AUC of 0.907 and accuracy 0.852, and the rebuilt, annotated network reproduces the original to within 4.4e-16. Self-probe of additivity on the typical person (a married husband, high-school graduate, professional specialty, no capital gains): the score is 0.957 (predicted chance 72%); with $10,000 of capital gains it is -4.405; never married and outside a family it is 3.527; with both changes it is -1.835, which is the typical score plus the two separate changes. On the probability scale the same marital change is worth much more for a person without gains (72% to 97%) than with $10,000 of gains (1.2% to 14%), because of the sigmoid. By ablation the parts rank: household (AUC 0.836 without it), capital gains (0.885), education (0.886), age, hours and work class (0.897), occupation (0.901), origin (0.9065) and the Italy branch (0.9069), against 0.9069 for the full model. The network's inputs with no connection (several work-class, education, occupation, relationship, race and country codes) have no effect and are entry nodes of this root.
ann_127.proposed: The model adds the scores of seven parts; for a typical person, higher capital gains lower the predicted chance of a low income slowly at first, then faster, more schooling lowers it in a curve highest at about 4 on the 1-16 scale, and being unmarried raises it from about 72% to about 97%.

parts.original_hypothesis: The model predicts the chance of a low income ($50,000 a year or less) as a sigmoid of a score that is a plain sum of the exits of the seven child parts and a bias; no part feeds another, so the parts' effects add on the score, and on the probability scale the sigmoid makes them interact. On the training split the model has an AUC of 0.907 and accuracy 0.852, and the rebuilt, annotated network reproduces the original to within 4.4e-16. Self-probe of additivity on the typical person (a married husband, high-school graduate, professional specialty, no capital gains): the score is 0.957 (predicted chance 72%); with $10,000 of capital gains it is -4.405; never married and outside a family it is 3.527; with both changes it is -1.835, which is the typical score plus the two separate changes. On the probability scale the same marital change is worth much more for a person without gains (72% to 97%) than with $10,000 of gains (1.2% to 14%), because of the sigmoid. By ablation the parts rank: household (AUC 0.836 without it), capital gains (0.885), education (0.886), age, hours and work class (0.897), occupation (0.901), origin (0.9065) and the Italy branch (0.9069), against 0.9069 for the full model. The network's inputs with no connection (several work-class, education, occupation, relationship, race and country codes) have no effect and are entry nodes of this root.

parts.name: capital_gains
parts.original_hypothesis: Capital gains pull the prediction away from a low income, and the pull steepens once gains pass about $4,000. Self-probe (the typical person: a married husband, high-school graduate, with no gains or losses, gains swept): this part's contribution to the low-income score goes from 1.36 at no gains to 0.60 at $3,500, -0.12 at $5,000 and -4.00 at $10,000: it falls slowly up to $3,500 and much faster beyond $5,000; in the whole model the predicted chance of a low income falls from 72% to 55%, 37% and 1.2%. The bend is two stacked hinges. Node 1266 is off at $3,500 (pre-activation -0.037) and on at $4,000 (0.028); node 8342, fed by 1266, is still off at $4,500 (pre-activation -0.037) and on at $5,000 (0.021). Both feed the output with negative weights, adding to the direct edge from capital gains (weight -3.11 per sd), while node 194 (capital-gain weight 1.24 per sd) feeds the output with a positive weight and gives back part of the direct edge's slope. In the training data 1266 is on for 2356 people, whose mean predicted chance of a low income is 17% (observed 20%), and 8342 for 2016 (mean predicted 10%). Every training row with gains of $4,000 or more has 1266 on (0 rows with it off); 70 rows just below $4,000 also have it on. Node 194 is zero on 50 training rows, and the 50 people born in Iran are those rows (Iran-born rows with 194 above zero: 0): the Iran indicator (weight -0.49 per sd into 194) shuts the node, so these people lose its offset, a regime fitted to 50 rows. Capital losses enter through one direct edge (weight -0.28 per sd): for the typical person, losses of $1,000 and $2,000 lower the predicted chance of a low income from 72% to 56% and 39%. Switching this part off lowers the training AUC from 0.907 to 0.885.
